sections.title: Architectural Representation: Stories and Strategies
sections.description: This course examines architectural representation as both a storytelling medium and a sociocultural practice, analyzing how drawings shape design ideologies, spatial narratives, and collective memory. Architectural imagery operates as both a tool of precision and a means of conceptual speculation, raising questions about whose stories are told through representation and how these narratives influence the built environment. Through critical engagement with historical and contemporary case studies, students will gain a deeper understanding of how architecture functions as a language of power, identity, and advocacy. The course begins with foundational works, contrasting Chinese isometric drawings, which challenge Western perspectival norms, with Giovanni Battista Piranesi’s Carceri d’Invenzione (1761), where spatial distortion imagines impossible architectures. It then expands representation’s role beyond architecture to examine W.E.B. Du Bois’s The Exhibit of American Negroes (1900), which reimagines data visualization as a form of spatial storytelling, demonstrating how non-traditional mediums critique power structures and expand architectural discourse. Frank Lloyd Wright’s Wasmuth Portfolio (1910) anchors a discussion on architectural imagery’s global influence, while Zaha Hadid’s axonometric experiments and Robin Evans’ Translations from Drawing to Building (1997) explore how abstraction mediates between idea and form. Modern case studies, including Mario Carpo’s The Alphabet and the Algorithm (2011), contextualize digital tools’ disruptive role in design. Through drawing workshops and discussions, students will experiment with collage, texture mapping, generative AI, and other mixed-media techniques to create representations that engage urgent themes of equity, identity, and ecology. The course culminates in critical writing reflections on architecture’s responsibility to amplify marginalized narratives and spatialize collective futures. By framing architectural representation as both a creative and ethical practice, students will develop design portfolios that go beyond technical skill, embracing architecture’s capacity to question, provoke, and advocate.
